extracted.intended_audience: college-level students (and instructors) learning to give and use peer review for academic writing
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for students (and instructors) on how to perform constructive peer review of academic writing and how authors should respond to reviewer feedback, including classroom peer review as an apprentice version of journal peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality (key point / thesis / purpose)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the key point that this author is trying to make? What is the central thesis? What is the purpose of this piece? Does this seem like a promising project to you? Why or why not? [Note: If you can’t figure out the key point, thesis or purpose, let the author know what you think it is and why you are unsure.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell the author whether you can identify their main claim and whether it seems significant or promising; if unclear, state what you think the key point is and why you're unsure. Use this to help the author refine or make their thesis more explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentation — development (evidence & support)
rubrics_metrics.description: How does the author develop this argument? Does it seem like there’s enough evidence to support the claims being made? Are there points that seem to need more support or explanation? [Note: If you are unconvinced by some points that are being presented – or think others will be unconvinced – explain why.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify gaps in evidence or explanation, note what additional sources or types of evidence might strengthen claims, and explain why you find particular claims unconvincing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Argumentation — arrangement (organization and flow)
rubrics_metrics.description: As you read through this piece from beginning to end, did the order in which points and information appeared seem sensible? Are there places where you felt lost or confused? Can you suggest a way to arrange material that might be more effective? [Note: Imagine an outline for the current version of the essay – does that outline seem logical or effective to you? What changes might you make?]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on macro-structure (sequence of sections, logical progression). If confused, propose reordering or restructuring; sketch an outline if helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability (style, sentence-level clarity, audience appropriateness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the style seem to suit the intended audience of this piece given its key goals? At the sentence level, is it easy to understand? At the word choice level, is the vocabulary appropriate for the subject matter and purpose of the essay? Are there small errors (formatting, etc.) that take attention away from the author’s ideas? [Note: This item is not an invitation to proofread or copy-edit. Try to focus only on places where you think a 'mistake' has a negative impact on the larger purpose of the essay.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess tone, register, clarity, and vocabulary relative to the intended audience; flag only those surface errors that impair comprehension or purpose rather than treating this as a full copyedit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall strengths, problems, and actionable suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Are there specific examples of strengths or problems you want to call to the attention of the author? Can you offer suggestions for what exactly the author might try to make this piece more effective? [Note: This is a place where you can comment on anything that didn’t get covered in the other four items on this list as well as make points that seem related to more than one element.]
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize major takeaways: what to keep, what to change, and concrete next steps (e.g., add X, cut Y, clarify Z). Provide examples of possible revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide constructive praise before criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s good practice to offer at least one major piece of constructive praise before presenting any criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start reviews by identifying something substantive that’s working and explain why — this orients the author to strengths they can build on and balances critiques so the author can see specific directions for revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer stance — be a collaborator not a judge
rubrics_metrics.description: See yourself as a collaborator in a larger project, one of many voices in an ongoing conversation about a topic. Think of yourself as a reader who wants to understand what the writer is trying to communicate and suggest ways they could do it more effectively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a helpful tone, avoid acting as the sole arbiter of correctness; offer suggestions and alternatives rather than commands; expect the author to make their own decisions about which suggestions to use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make feedback specific and actionable
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer specific recommendations of what the author might try alongside any criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead of vague comments like 'unclear' or 'bad paragraph,' point to the passage and suggest concrete revisions (e.g., 'move this example earlier,' 'add a sentence linking A to B,' 'define this term').

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Reviewer Two behaviors (mean, unhelpful, or unreasonable feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not write vicious comments, personal attacks, or demands for impossible new research. Avoid rejecting a submission while failing to engage the basic point, or insisting on changes that are infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use anonymity as cover for cruelty. If a reviewer’s reaction is negative, try to explain why and how the author might respond; don’t belittle the author or their competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize global issues before local fixes in revision planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan revision tasks so you tackle big structural or conceptual changes before small details (e.g., manage global structural revisions before worrying about small details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Order planned responses (easy tasks first or big jobs first depending on strategy), and make a to-do list that sequences work so revision is manageable and efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus reviewer attention at a high level (avoid nitpicking)
rubrics_metrics.description: When giving peer review, stay at a high level of praise and criticism rather than getting bogged down in minor details on a first pass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Save detailed copy-editing for later rounds; initial peer review should prioritize purpose, argument, evidence, and organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesize and prioritize multiple readers’ feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn feedback from different readers (peers, tutors, instructor) into a formal plan for revision; reconcile contradictory advice and decide which changes to adopt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a chart or list to note each comment, judge validity, and plan responses; when advice conflicts, reflect on authorial goals and intended audience to choose the best path.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection and validation of reviewer comments (as author)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you receive feedback, reflect on whether each comment is valid and how you will respond. Keep in mind that a peer reviewer can be wrong, but even a bad comment can prompt useful thinking about revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freewrite an initial emotional response, then create a planned response that evaluates the comment's validity and maps it to specific revision actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create a revision plan / chart
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a chart listing features evaluated, peer-reviewer comment, reflection (valid or not), and planned response (and optional ordering/prioritization).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter provides a sample filled-in chart and a blank template inspired by Belcher; use this to convert comments into ordered tasks and to track what you will (and won’t) change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to harsh feedback with a growth mindset
rubrics_metrics.description: Face upsetting comments by assuming you can learn to revise and by planning a constructive response rather than abandoning the project or taking criticism as a final verdict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use emotional-processing techniques (freewriting then planned response), identify salvageable suggestions, and turn negative feedback into specific revision strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with relevant research / examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the piece engages appropriate sources and examples and whether more or different sources/explanations are needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest additional literature to cite, question over-reliance on one type of evidence, and recommend ways to integrate sources so claims are better supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor/reviewer decision criteria for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: For journal peer review: assess whether the key idea is original, makes a meaningful contribution to the field, and is well-supported; reviewers also comment on what to define, what sources to reference, errors to correct, and give an overall recommendation (accept, reject, or revise-and-resubmit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating for publication, explicitly address originality, contribution, evidentiary support, accuracy, and ethical issues; offer a clear recommendation and rationale to editors.
